units.title: Unit 21 — Clothes
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 21. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Name common clothes, jewellery and garment parts shown in the unit illustrations.
Distinguish stylish, well-dressed, smartly dressed and casual in context.
Use get dressed, wear, put on, take off, undo, do up and change into correctly.
Explain how colours suit people and how someone looks in particular clothes.
Use plural clothing nouns and a pair of appropriately.

items.example: She chose a stylish jacket for the party.
items.note: Describes clothes or people with an attractive, fashionable appearance.

items.example: The guests were smartly dressed for the ceremony.
items.note: Describes a neat, tidy appearance suitable for a formal occasion.

items.example: His colleagues are always well-dressed at work.
items.note: Describes a person who wears attractive or suitable clothes.

items.example: You can wear casual clothes at the weekend.
items.note: Casual clothes are suitable for informal situations rather than formal events.

items.pt: blusa; peça de roupa da parte superior
items.example: I bought a blue top to wear with these trousers.
items.note: A general word for clothing worn on the upper body.

items.example: He usually wears a T-shirt when he goes cycling.
items.note: A casual shirt, typically with short sleeves and no collar.

items.example: Take a jumper because the evenings are cold.
items.note: British English for a warm knitted item worn over the upper body.

items.example: She wore a thick sweater on the journey.
items.note: An alternative to jumper; sweater is common in American English too.

items.example: My jacket has two pockets and a zip.
items.note: An item of outer clothing covering the upper body.

items.example: My old jeans are still very comfortable.
items.note: A plural-form noun; say these jeans or a pair of jeans.

items.example: The skirt is too long for me.
items.note: A garment hanging from the waist.

items.example: She wore thick tights with her skirt.
items.note: A plural-form noun; say a pair of tights for one item.

items.example: Wear your boots if the ground is wet.
items.note: Footwear that covers the foot and extends above the ankle.

items.example: These trainers are comfortable for walking.
items.note: British English; American English usually uses sneakers.

items.example: He put on a cap to protect his eyes from the sun.
items.note: A soft hat, often with a peak at the front.

items.example: She wrapped a scarf around her neck.
items.note: A piece of fabric worn around the neck or head.

items.example: I never wear a tie unless I have an important meeting.
items.note: A narrow piece of fabric tied around the neck with a shirt.

items.example: He bought a new suit for the interview.
items.note: A noun for a matching jacket and trousers or skirt, usually formal.

items.example: She carries her laptop in a rucksack.
items.note: British English for a bag carried on the back with two straps.

items.example: He found a silver earring on the floor.
items.note: An item of jewellery worn on an ear; often used in the plural, earrings.

items.example: She received a necklace for her birthday.
items.note: An item of jewellery worn around the neck.

items.example: My sister wears a bracelet on her left wrist.
items.note: An item of jewellery worn around the wrist.

items.example: He wears a simple gold ring.
items.note: An item of jewellery worn on a finger.

items.example: The collar of his shirt was folded neatly.
items.note: The part of a shirt or jacket around the neck.

items.example: There's a small mark on the sleeve of my coat.
items.note: The part of a garment that covers an arm.

items.example: I keep my keys in my jacket pocket.
items.note: A small sewn-in bag in clothing used to hold objects.

items.example: One button has fallen off my shirt.
items.note: A small fastening used to close a garment.

items.example: The zip on this bag is broken.
items.note: British English for a sliding fastening; American English often uses zipper.

items.example: I packed some warm clothes for the trip.
items.note: Always plural in ordinary use: clothes are; not a clothe for one garment.

items.example: These trousers are too long for me.
items.note: A plural-form noun in British English: trousers are, or a pair of trousers.

items.example: She keeps her jewellery in a small box.
items.note: Uncountable in standard English: some jewellery, not jewelleries.

items.example: I get dressed after I have a shower.
items.note: Means put your clothes on; get dressed does not require an object.

items.example: Do you have to wear a uniform at work?
items.note: Wear describes having clothes on your body, not the action of putting them on.

items.pt: vestir; colocar uma peça de roupa
items.example: Put your coat on before you go outside.
items.note: Separable: put it on, not put on it; contrasts with take something off.

items.example: Please take your muddy boots off at the door.
items.note: Separable: take them off, not take off them.

items.pt: abrir um zíper; desabotoar ou desfazer um fecho
items.example: I had to undo the zip before taking off my jacket.
items.note: Undo means unfasten something, including a zip, button or tie.

items.example: Could you do up the zip on my coat?
items.note: Do up means fasten; you can also do up buttons. This verb is separable.

items.pt: trocar de roupa; vestir outra roupa
items.example: She changed into comfortable clothes after work.
items.note: Change into introduces the new clothes you put on.

items.pt: cair bem em alguém; combinar com alguém
items.example: I think green suits you very well.
items.note: For appearance, suit means look good on someone. It does not mean be the right size.

items.pt: ficar bem usando determinada roupa ou cor
items.example: He looks good in dark blue.
items.note: The person is the subject: someone looks good in a colour or garment.

items.example: I prefer dark colours for winter clothes.
items.note: Contrasts with bright colours; British spelling: colours.

items.example: Bright colours can make an outfit more cheerful.
items.note: Colours that are strong or vivid, unlike dark colours.

items.example: I need a new pair of jeans for the weekend.
items.note: Use a pair of with jeans and trousers when referring to one item.

sectionsChecked: A: Smart, stylish and casual; labelled clothing illustrations
B: Verbs and phrases used with clothes; common mistakes

units.title: Unit 22 — Fashion and buying clothes
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 22. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Talk about shopping for clothes, current fashions and designer labels.
Distinguish matching and going with, and distinguish fit from suit.
Describe clothing sizes using tight, loose and bigger size.
Ask for help, try clothes on and respond politely to shop assistants.
Choose natural expressions for buying or leaving an item.

items.example: I usually shop online for basic clothes.
items.note: Shop is a verb meaning buy or look for things in shops.

items.example: We're going shopping for winter clothes tomorrow.
items.note: A common equivalent of shop; use go + -ing for this activity.

items.example: Can I try these shoes on before buying them?
items.note: Try on means put clothes on to see how they look or fit; separable: try it on.

items.example: Those trainers were fashionable last year.
items.note: Describes something currently popular in fashion.

items.example: Loose trousers are in fashion at the moment.
items.note: Similar in meaning to fashionable; contrasts with out of fashion.

items.example: Her wardrobe is full of winter coats.
items.note: A large cupboard for storing clothes; also used for someone's collection of clothes.

items.pt: marca de grife; marca de estilista
items.example: You don't need a designer label to look smart.
items.note: Clothing from a well-known fashion designer, often expensive.

items.example: The quality is good and the price is reasonable.
items.note: In relation to prices, reasonable means not too expensive.

items.pt: combinar com algo; ficar bem junto com algo
items.example: Does this shirt go with my grey jacket?
items.note: Describes clothes or accessories that look good together; close to match.

items.pt: combinar com algo; ter cor ou estilo correspondente
items.example: Her shoes match her handbag.
items.note: Often means two things have a similar or coordinated colour or style.

items.pt: vestir-se com determinado tipo de roupa ou cor
items.example: For special occasions, he likes to dress in dark colours.
items.note: Describes the kind or colour of clothes someone chooses to wear.

items.example: I can't remember what I had on at the party.
items.note: Informal phrase meaning be wearing a particular item of clothing.

items.pt: servir em alguém; ter o tamanho adequado
items.example: This coat fits me, but I don't like its colour.
items.note: Fit means be the correct size, while suit means look attractive on a person.

items.pt: ficar bem em alguém; cair bem em alguém
items.example: That colour looks good on your sister.
items.note: With clothes as the subject, use look good on someone; compare someone looks good in clothes.

items.pt: atendente de loja; vendedor de loja
items.example: A shop assistant showed us the jackets on sale.
items.note: British English term for a person employed to help customers in a shop.

items.example: The customer asked for a different size.
items.note: A person who buys or is considering buying something.

items.example: A member of staff came to serve the next customer.
items.note: Serve means help a person buy goods in a shop.

items.example: When another assistant offered help, I said, “I'm being served.”
items.note: A polite way to say another shop assistant is already helping you.

items.example: These sleeves are too tight around my arms.
items.note: Opposite: loose; a tight garment leaves very little room.

items.example: I prefer loose shirts in hot weather.
items.note: Opposite: tight. Loose clothes do not fit closely to the body.

items.example: Do you have this jacket in my size?
items.note: In clothing shops, size refers to a standard measurement or number.

items.example: Could I see a bigger size, please?
items.note: A useful polite shopping phrase when the garment is too small.

items.example: The changing room is at the back of the shop.
items.note: A space where customers try on clothes before buying.

items.example: They didn't have my size, so I said, “That's a shame.”
items.note: A natural response to disappointing news; similar to That's a pity.

items.example: “The shop is closed today.” “That's a pity.”
items.note: A synonym of That's a shame when something is disappointing.

items.pt: Vou deixar; não vou levar, obrigado.
items.example: The jacket was uncomfortable, so I said, “I'll leave it, thanks.”
items.note: A polite refusal to buy an item; opposite: I'll take it.

items.pt: Vou levar; vou ficar com isso.
items.example: The jacket fits perfectly, so I'll take it.
items.note: Tells the assistant you have decided to buy the item; for several items, say I'll take them.

items.pt: procurar algo; estar em busca de algo
items.example: I'm looking for a warm coat for my daughter.
items.note: Look for means try to find; commonly used as I'm looking for ... in shops.

items.example: The assistant smiled and asked, “Can I help you?”
items.note: A standard offer of assistance from shop staff.

items.example: A shop assistant asked whether I needed any help.
items.note: Another standard offer of help in a shop.

items.example: I pointed to the shirt and asked, “Can I try it on?”
items.note: A request to try a garment before buying; it is placed between try and on.

items.example: I'm afraid we don't have that colour today.
items.note: A polite introduction to disappointing or negative information, not necessarily an expression of fear.

items.example: The coat looks lovely, but it's too expensive.
items.note: Expensive means costing a lot of money; reasonable can describe an acceptable price.

sectionsChecked: A: Fashion; matching, suitability and size contrasts
B: In a clothes shop; dialogue and expressions
